Baby & Child

Language Activities for Toddlers: Games by Age

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The best language activities for toddlers are simple back-and-forth games: respond to your child's sounds, name what they are looking at, and add one or two words to whatever they say. Researchers call this serve and return, and it builds language better than flashcards or fancy toys. Every game below takes zero prep and fits into the next ten minutes of an ordinary day.

The one rule behind every game: serve and return

Every game in this guide works because of one idea: serve and return. Your child serves by babbling, pointing, reaching, or looking at something. You return by responding with words, a smile, or a turn in the game. Child development researchers, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and Harvard's Center on the Developing Child, describe these back-and-forth exchanges as the foundation of early language. The returns matter more than the toys; a cardboard box with a chatty parent beats an expensive talking toy. So before you memorize any activity, practice the habit underneath it: notice what your child is paying attention to, respond to it, then pause and wait for them to take another turn.

Two techniques from speech therapy make the returns easy. Self-talk means narrating what you are doing: 'I am cutting the apple. Now it goes in the bowl.' Parallel talk means narrating what your child is doing: 'You found the ball. You are rolling it.' Neither one asks for an answer, which is the point. You are giving your child a steady stream of words tied to things they can see and touch, with no pressure to perform. Aim for more comments than questions. Quizzing a toddler with 'what is this, what color is that' tires everyone out. Describing the world together keeps the game going.

6 to 12 months: games for babblers

Peekaboo is a language game in disguise. It teaches turn-taking, the rhythm of conversation, and the thrill of guessing what comes next. Play it with your hands, a blanket, or around the edge of the sofa, and pause a little longer each round so your baby learns to wait for a turn. The copycat game is just as simple: when your baby babbles 'ba ba', repeat it back, then wait. Many babies will say it again, and now you are having your first conversation. You can also serve first: make a sound like 'ooo' or a tongue click, and watch whether your baby tries a version of it.

Naming body parts fits into routines you already do. During a diaper change or bath, touch a foot and say 'foot', touch the tummy and say 'tummy'. Keep it slow and repetitive; babies learn from hearing the same word in the same moment many times. Singing works even better when you add pauses. Pick any song your baby knows well, stop just before a favorite word, and wait with an expectant face. Over weeks, many babies start filling the gap with a sound, a bounce, or a gesture. That fill-in is a real conversational turn, so celebrate it and keep singing.

12 to 18 months: first words at work

Turn walks, even ten steps to the mailbox, into point-and-name walks. Follow your toddler's pointing finger and name whatever caught their eye: 'Bus. A big bus.' Short phrases beat full sentences at this age, because your child can pick out the important word. Animal sounds make great early words, since 'moo' and 'woof' are easier to say than 'cow' and 'dog'. Look at animals in books, out the window, or in the toy bin, make the sound, and pause so your toddler can try it. Producing the sound instead of the word still counts as talking, so treat it like the real thing.

Offering two choices out loud puts words to work. Hold up both options and ask, 'banana or yogurt?', then wait. Any answer counts: a point, a reach, a grunt, or a word, and you respond by naming the choice: 'Banana. You picked the banana.' Simple pretend play often starts to appear around this age too. Hand your toddler a toy phone or an empty cup, hold your own, and model a tiny script: a cheerful 'hello' and 'bye bye', or a loud pretend sip followed by 'mmm, water'. These little routines give your child words with a job to do, which is how words stick.

18 to 24 months: stretching words into phrases

The expansion game is the workhorse of this stage, and speech therapists teach it to parents everywhere. When your child says a word, say it back with one or two words added. 'Dog' becomes 'yes, a big brown dog'. 'Car go' becomes 'the car is going fast'. You are confirming that the message landed, then showing the next step up, all without correcting anyone. If a word comes out garbled, resist saying 'no, say it like this'. Just use the correct version naturally in your reply. Expansions work in any language you speak at home, so use whichever one feels most comfortable in the moment.

Picture hunts turn any book, flyer, or catalog into a game: 'Where is the cat? Can you find the ball?' Let your child hunt, name the find together, and add one detail: 'You found the cat. A sleepy cat.' Narrating chores works the same magic with zero extra time. Sorting laundry becomes a color and size game, unloading groceries becomes a naming parade, and wiping the table becomes 'wet, dry, all clean'. If you enjoy keeping track, jot new words in BeMama or on a note on the fridge. Watching the list grow is encouraging on days when progress feels invisible.

2 to 3 years: silly games and real conversations

Two year olds love catching grown-ups being wrong, so make silly mistakes on purpose. Put a sock on your hand and announce 'my mitten', point to the dog and say 'what a nice cow', or hand over a spoon when they asked for a fork. The delighted correction that follows is exactly the kind of confident talking you want to hear. I-spy works well once you swap letters for descriptions: 'I spy something round and red', or 'something soft that says meow'. Description games stretch listening skills and hand your child a model for describing things in their own words later.

Reading time is a conversation waiting to happen. Instead of reading straight through, pause and ask open questions: 'What do you think happens next?' 'Why is she sad?' 'What would you do?' Then wait longer than feels natural; two year olds often need several seconds to build an answer. Follow wherever their answer leads, even if you never finish the book. Remember that these games are support, not a test, and children learn to talk on wonderfully different schedules. If something about your child's speech or hearing worries you, bring it up with your pediatrician or family doctor rather than waiting for the worry to fade.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Language grows through responsive interaction: talking, listening, naming, singing, shared reading, and taking turns in play. Everyday conversation in the family’s strongest languages supports connection and learning.

Milestone ranges vary, but loss of language, limited response to sound or name, or caregiver concern should be discussed with a healthcare professional and may warrant hearing or developmental assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to save favourite activities, new words, and questions for well-child visits. It cannot screen hearing, speech, or language development.

When to seek help

Request professional assessment when communication concerns persist or a child loses previously used words or social skills.

Sources and further reading

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Respond to your child's sounds, looks, and points; the back-and-forth teaches more than any toy.
  • Match the game to the stage: copycat sounds for babies, naming games around one year, expansions for older toddlers.
  • Add one or two words to whatever your child says instead of correcting them.
  • Narrate ordinary routines with self-talk and parallel talk; comments beat quizzes.
  • Ten minutes of playful back-and-forth a day beats a long teaching session.

Frequently asked questions

How can I encourage my 1 year old to talk?

Copy your one year old's sounds, name whatever they point at, and leave long pauses so they can take a turn. Offer two choices out loud at meals, then treat any response, a point, a reach, or a sound, as a real answer. Short phrases of one to three words are easier to learn from than full sentences. Gestures and animal sounds count as communication at this age, so respond to them the way you would respond to words.

What is serve and return with babies?

Serve and return is the back-and-forth exchange between a baby and a caregiver: the baby serves with a babble, look, or point, and the adult returns with words, a smile, or a turn in a game. Child development researchers describe these exchanges as the foundation of early brain and language growth. Peekaboo, copycat sounds, and naming whatever your baby is looking at are all serve and return in action.

What are good talking games for 2 year olds?

Good talking games for 2 year olds include making silly mistakes for them to correct, playing I-spy with descriptions instead of letters, and asking open questions during picture books. Add the expansion game throughout the day: repeat what your child says with one or two words added. Keep each game short and playful, and stop while it is still fun.

How do I build my toddler's vocabulary?

The fastest way to build toddler vocabulary is to talk about what your child is already paying attention to, then expand whatever they say by one or two words. Point-and-name walks, narrated chores, and picture hunts tie new words to real objects and actions. Repetition helps, so use the same words in the same routines every day. New books and new outings add fresh words once the familiar ones stick.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
